final_proof:
Let \(M\) be locally Euclidean of dimension \(d\), and fix \(m\in M\). By local Euclideanness, there are an open neighborhood \(V\) of \(m\), an open set \(O\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and a homeomorphism
\[
\varphi:V\longrightarrow O.
\]
Put \(x=\varphi(m)\). Since \(O\) is open and contains \(x\), there is some \(r>0\) such that the Euclidean open ball \(B(x,r)\) is contained in \(O\).

For each \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(n\geq 1\), define
\[
U_n=\varphi^{-1}\bigl(B(x,r/n)\bigr).
\]
(If the convention is that \(0\in\mathbb N\), set \(U_0=U_1\).) Because \(B(x,r/n)\) is open in \(O\) and \(\varphi\) is a homeomorphism, \(U_n\) is open in \(V\); and because \(V\) is open in \(M\), \(U_n\) is open in \(M\). Moreover, \(m\in U_n\). Thus every \(U_n\) is a neighborhood of \(m\). The restriction
\[
\varphi^{-1}\big|_{B(x,r/n)}:B(x,r/n)\longrightarrow U_n
\]
is a homeomorphism, so each \(U_n\) is the homeomorphic image of an open ball in \(\mathbb R^d\).

It remains to verify the local-basis property. Let \(N\) be any neighborhood of \(m\). By the definition of neighborhood, there is an open set \(G\subseteq M\) such that \(m\in G\subseteq N\). The set \(G\cap V\) is open in \(V\) and contains \(m\), so \(\varphi(G\cap V)\) is an open subset of \(\mathbb R^d\) containing \(x\). Hence there is \(\varepsilon>0\) such that
\[
B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq \varphi(G\cap V).
\]
By the Archimedean property, choose \(n\geq1\) with \(r/n<\varepsilon\). Then
\[
U_n=\varphi^{-1}(B(x,r/n))
\subseteq \varphi^{-1}(B(x,\varepsilon))
\subseteq G\cap V
\subseteq N.
\]
Thus every neighborhood of \(m\) contains some \(U_n\). Therefore \(\{U_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is a countable local basis at \(m\), and all of its members are homeomorphic images of open balls in \(\mathbb R^d\), as required.
